opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I don't think the plan is crazy. In some ways it's the only plan that really makes sense given where we are. If you have AI systems that are getting very capable at research, it's natural to want to point them at the alignment problem. My worry is less that the idea is wrong in principle and more about how it's likely to play out in practice.

The core issue, I think, is timing and competitive pressure. The vision is roughly: we get AIs that are good enough to do a lot of alignment research, they help us solve the hard problems, and then we can safely build the more powerful systems after that. But the same capabilities that make an AI good at alignment research also make it good at capabilities research, and at basically everything else economically valuable. So the moment you have those systems, there's enormous pressure to use them to go faster on everything. The fraction of that AI labor that actually goes to safety could easily be small, especially if a company thinks its competitors aren't slowing down.

And the period where this has to work might be really short. If AI is automating AI R&D, you could go from "AIs are a useful research assistant" to "AIs are much smarter than us" in maybe a year or two, possibly less. So you need the alignment work to be fast enough to keep pace with a capabilities explosion that's being driven by the same engine. That's a hard race to win if you're not deliberately prioritizing it.

The second issue is verification. Alignment research is unusually hard to check. With a lot of capabilities work, you get a clear feedback signal: did the model get better at the benchmark, did the code run, did the loss go down. With alignment, the thing you most care about is whether the model is actually trustworthy in situations you can't directly observe, and whether a proposed technique really works or just looks like it works. If you're relying on AI systems to produce that research, and you're not sure those systems are themselves aligned, then you're in this awkward position of trusting possibly untrustworthy systems to tell you whether they're trustworthy. Even without anything adversarial going on, you could get a lot of research that looks plausible and convincing but doesn't hold up, and humans may not be able to tell the difference at the speed things are moving.

So when I put those together, the most likely failure mode in my mind isn't some dramatic scenario where the AI clearly sabotages the effort. It's more mundane: companies don't allocate enough of their AI labor to safety, the window is shorter than they expected, the outputs are hard to evaluate, and they end up proceeding with more powerful systems on the basis of evidence that's a lot weaker than it should be.

What would make me more optimistic is if companies committed in advance to concrete things, like a specific share of compute or AI labor going to alignment and security once certain capability thresholds are hit, and a willingness to actually slow down if the safety work isn't keeping up. Right now it often feels like "we'll use AI to solve alignment" is doing a lot of work in the plan without much specification of what that looks like when the pressure is on.

r001.rationale: The response identifies companies’ likely failure to direct enough AI labor toward safety, given pressure to use capable systems to advance everything else, as a central failure mode.

r002.rationale: It says companies may devote little AI labor to safety because competitors may keep advancing, creating pressure to move faster on other work.

r003.rationale: It says alignment work must keep pace with a capabilities explosion, but does not state that absolute safety labor could increase and still be insufficient.

r004.rationale: It proposes advance commitments by companies to devote a share of compute or AI labor to safety, but does not propose an agreement among competing companies to protect their relative competitive positions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I actually think the basic idea is pretty reasonable. If you're going to get a huge amount of cognitive labor from AI systems at some point, it would be strange not to point some of it at alignment. So I'm not saying the plan is crazy. I'm saying I think the most likely way it fails is kind of boring, and it's not the dramatic failure people usually picture.

The dramatic version is: you ask your AI to do alignment research, and it's secretly misaligned, and it sandbags or sabotages the work, and you can't tell. That's a real concern and I don't want to dismiss it. But I think there's an earlier and more mundane failure mode, which is that the plan just quietly never gets executed in the form that was promised, because the incentives at the moment it matters all point the other way.

Here's what I mean. The whole pitch is: we'll build systems that are somewhat more capable than us, and then we'll pause, or at least slow down, and spend a big chunk of that capability on making the next generation safe before we build it. But think about what the world looks like at that moment. You have a model that can do a large fraction of the work of an ML research engineer. Your competitors have something comparable, or you believe they do. The commercial value of using that model to make the next model better is enormous and very legible. The value of using it to do alignment research is real, but it's diffuse, it's harder to measure, and it doesn't show up on anyone's quarterly numbers. So the "pause and do alignment" step gets compressed. It becomes a few weeks instead of a year. It becomes ten percent of compute instead of fifty. Every individual decision to shave a little off looks defensible, and the sum of them is that the plan doesn't happen.

And the second piece is that alignment research, unlike capabilities research, doesn't have a clean feedback loop. If you're trying to make the model better at coding, you can measure that. The automated researcher can run a thousand experiments and the ones that work get kept. If you're trying to make the model honest, or trying to make sure it isn't scheming, you don't have a ground-truth signal in the same way. You're often trying to find problems in a regime where you can't easily verify the answer. So even an AI that's genuinely trying its best is working on a problem where it's much easier to produce plausible-looking output than to produce output that's actually correct. And then humans have to evaluate that output, and we're already the bottleneck, and now there's a lot more of it.

So you put those together. You've got a shrinking time window, a research problem with weak feedback, and humans who are supposed to be checking the work but are being asked to check far more than they can. In that situation I think the most likely outcome isn't that the AI betrays you. It's that you end up with a lot of nice-looking alignment research that nobody had time to really verify, and a sense that the problem is handled because so much work was done on it. That's the failure I worry about most. Not sabotage. Just a plan that gets eaten by the pressures of the moment it was designed for.

The thing that would make me more optimistic is seeing companies commit now, when it's cheap, to concrete and verifiable allocations. Like, actual numbers on compute and time, with some external party who can check. Because if you can't commit to it when the stakes are low, I don't think you'll suddenly manage it when they're high.

r001.rationale: It identifies the central failure as companies failing to carry out the promised shift of AI effort toward alignment, with capability work winning out.

r002.rationale: It explains that competitive pressure and the clear commercial value of improving the next model make companies less likely to devote substantial effort to alignment.

r003.rationale: It describes alignment work being compressed and possibly unverified, but does not say that an increase in the absolute amount of safety labor could still be inadequate relative to the pace of AI advancement.

r004.rationale: It proposes verifiable company commitments to compute and time, but does not propose an agreement among competing companies to prevent them from losing relative competitive position by allocating compute to safety.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is that getting useful alignment research out of an AI is different from knowing that the research actually makes a more capable system safe. You can imagine the AI producing a very compelling proposal, writing the code, running experiments, and showing you results that look reassuring. But if there’s a flaw that neither you nor your AI assistants can reliably recognize, you haven’t solved the underlying problem.

And there’s a bootstrapping issue: you want to use AI because it can do work that humans can’t easily do ourselves. But that also makes the work harder to supervise. You need some reason to trust the system doing the research, or a way to check its outputs that doesn’t depend on already having solved alignment. Otherwise, you risk moving the hard part from “build an aligned AI” to “trust this other AI’s judgment about alignment.”

I don’t think that means AI assistance is useless. It could be enormously valuable. What worries me is a plan where the assistance gets more powerful, the pace gets faster, and our ability to distinguish actual safety from the appearance of safety doesn’t keep up. Especially under competitive pressure, I think it’s very easy for “we haven’t found a problem” to become “we’ve demonstrated that this is safe.”

r001.rationale: The response focuses on verifying AI-generated alignment work and supervising capable systems; it does not identify insufficient redirection of AI labor from capability work to safety as the likely failure.

r002.rationale: It mentions competitive pressure, but does not say that this pressure discourages companies from allocating substantial AI labor to safety.

r003.rationale: It says AI assistance and its pace may outstrip the ability to distinguish safety from its appearance, but does not state that safety labor could increase and still lag AI advancement.

r004.rationale: The response proposes no agreement among competing companies to allocate compute to safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest risk is that we get AI systems that are very good at producing alignment research that looks convincing to us, before we get systems whose research we can actually trust.

The basic plan has a lot going for it: if AI can automate programming and scientific research, we should use that capability to help solve alignment. But the hard part is knowing whether the work it produces is actually solving the problem. We’re asking for help precisely because we don’t fully understand how to evaluate whether a much more capable system is aligned. So there’s a danger of using our own judgment as the training signal and getting systems that are excellent at satisfying that judgment, without actually making us safer.

And you don’t even need deliberate deception for that to go wrong. A model could suggest experiments, get encouraging results, and write persuasive explanations, while missing problems that only emerge when the next system is more capable or operating in a different setting. If it is deliberately deceiving us, then the same evaluation gap gives it room to steer the research in ways we won’t notice.

So the question I’d want companies to answer is: what evidence would distinguish an AI that’s genuinely helping us solve alignment from one that’s producing work we’re inclined to approve of? I’m much more optimistic about using AI on pieces where we have strong, independent checks. I’m much less comfortable with a plan where the central assurance is that the AI’s alignment research looks good to the people building the next model.

r001.rationale: The response identifies an evaluation gap and persuasive but untrustworthy research as the main risk. It does not identify insufficiently redirecting AI labor from capability work to safety.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss competitive pressure to stay ahead or how it limits companies’ allocation of AI labor to safety.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the amount of safety labor with the pace of AI advancement.

r004.rationale: The response proposes no agreement among companies to allocate compute to safety.
